books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, B. The Market Revolution's Impact on Economic Class

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 B: In the 1830s, the mill workers in Lowell, Massachusetts, staged two strikes. In 1834, the women staged an unsuccessful “turn-out” to protest a wage cut. Two years later, organized as the Factory Girls Association, they had greater success protesting a rent increase in the boardinghouses. In 1842, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decided Commonwealth v. Hunt, declaring that unions were lawful organizations as long as they used legal means — including striking — to achieve their goals.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.6 B. Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The decision in Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842) mattered to American workers because it

options.text: declared unions lawful as long as they used legal means
banned all strikes by factory workers
options.misconception: The court ruled the other way: unions were lawful, and striking was a legal means.

options.text: set a minimum wage for mill workers by law
options.misconception: The case was about whether unions were lawful, not about wage levels.

options.text: gave women the right to join men's unions
options.misconception: The case decided the legality of unions generally; it said nothing about women joining men's unions.

rationales.A: Commonwealth v. Hunt held that a union was lawful when it used legal means to reach its goals, and striking counted as a legal means. Workers could organize without being charged with conspiracy.
rationales.B: The court did not ban strikes. It said striking was a legal means for a lawful union.
rationales.C: No wage appears in the decision. The case settled whether unions were criminal conspiracies, not what workers must be paid.
rationales.D: The case was about unions in general, decided by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court. It did not rule on women joining men's unions.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the court decided. Unions are lawful organizations when they use legal means.
2. Ask what counts as legal. Striking counts, the court said.
3. Ask why it mattered. Before this, unions could be charged as criminal conspiracies.
Background: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decided the case in 1842, setting a precedent other states followed.
Remember: a court case matters for the rule it sets, so state the rule.
